verses.t: A man of Ren asked Wulu Zi, "Which is more important, ritual or food?" "Ritual is more important." "Which is more important, sex or ritual?" "Ritual is more important." "If by observing the rites in eating one would starve to death, while by ignoring them one would get food, must one still observe the rites? If by going in person to fetch one's bride one would not get a wife, while by not going one would get a wife, must one still go in person?" Wulu Zi could not answer. The next day he went to Zou and told Mencius. Mencius said, "What difficulty is there in answering this? If you do not measure the base but only level off the tops, a piece of wood an inch square can be made higher than a tall tower. When we say gold is heavier than feathers, do we mean a single clasp of gold and a whole cartload of feathers? If you take the weightiest matters of food and compare them with the lightest matters of ritual, why stop at saying food is more important? If you take the weightiest matters of sex and compare them with the lightest matters of ritual, why stop at saying sex is more important? Go and answer him: 'If by twisting your elder brother's arm and snatching his food you could get food, while by not twisting it you would get none, would you twist it? If by climbing over your eastern neighbor's wall and dragging off his daughter you could get a wife, while by not doing so you would get none, would you drag her off?'"

Cao Jiao asked, "Is it true that all people can become a Yao or a Shun?" Mencius said, "It is." "I have heard that King Wen was ten feet tall and Tang nine feet. Now I am nine feet four inches tall, yet all I do is eat grain. What should I do?" "What does that have to do with it? You simply have to do it. Here is a man who cannot lift a duckling; he is a man without strength. If he says he can lift a hundred jun, he is a man of strength. Then whoever can lift the load that Wu Huo lifted is simply another Wu Huo. Why should a person worry about not being equal to a task? It is only that he does not do it. Walking slowly behind one's elders is called being a good younger brother; walking quickly ahead of one's elders is called being a bad younger brother. Is walking slowly something a person cannot do? It is only that he does not do it. The Way of Yao and Shun is nothing but filial piety and brotherly respect. If you wear the clothes of Yao, speak the words of Yao, and do the deeds of Yao, you are simply Yao. If you wear the clothes of Jie, speak the words of Jie, and do the deeds of Jie, you are simply Jie." Cao Jiao said, "I could get an audience with the ruler of Zou and borrow a lodging there. I would like to stay and receive instruction at your gate." Mencius said, "The Way is like a great road; how is it hard to know? People's trouble is only that they do not seek it. Go home and seek it, and you will find teachers enough."

Gongsun Chou asked, "Gaozi says that 'The Small Cap' is the ode of a petty man." Mencius said, "Why does he say so?" "Because it is resentful." Mencius said, "How rigid old Gao is in reading the Odes! Suppose a man from Yue bends his bow to shoot someone: one can talk about it laughing, for no other reason than that he is a stranger. But if one's own elder brother bends his bow to shoot someone, one talks about it in tears, for no other reason than that he is kin. The resentment in 'The Small Cap' comes from loving one's kin, and loving one's kin is benevolence. How rigid old Gao is in reading the Odes!" "Why then is there no resentment in 'The Gentle Breeze'?" "In 'The Gentle Breeze' the parent's fault is small; in 'The Small Cap' the parent's fault is great. Not to resent a parent's great fault is to grow more distant from them; to resent a parent's small fault is to be unable to bear the slightest irritation. To grow more distant is unfilial, and to be unable to bear the slightest irritation is also unfilial. Confucius said, 'Shun was the most filial of men: at fifty he still yearned for his parents.'"

Song Keng was on his way to Chu, and Mencius met him at Shiqiu. Mencius said, "Where are you going, sir?" "I hear that Qin and Chu are taking up arms against each other. I am going to see the king of Chu and persuade him to stop. If the king of Chu is not pleased, I will go to see the king of Qin and persuade him to stop. With one of the two kings I shall surely succeed." Mencius said, "I will not ask about the details, but I would like to hear the gist. How will you persuade them?" "I will tell them it is not profitable." Mencius said, "Your purpose, sir, is great, but your slogan will not do. If you persuade the kings of Qin and Chu with profit, and they, delighted with profit, call off their armies, then the soldiers of the armies will be glad to stop and will delight in profit. Ministers will serve their rulers with profit in mind, sons will serve their fathers with profit in mind, and younger brothers will serve their elder brothers with profit in mind. Thus ruler and minister, father and son, elder and younger brother will at last cast off benevolence and righteousness and deal with one another with profit in mind. No state like that has ever failed to perish. If you persuade the kings of Qin and Chu with benevolence and righteousness, and they, delighted with benevolence and righteousness, call off their armies, then the soldiers will be glad to stop and will delight in benevolence and righteousness. Ministers will serve their rulers with benevolence and righteousness in mind, sons will serve their fathers, and younger brothers their elder brothers, with benevolence and righteousness in mind. Thus ruler and minister, father and son, elder and younger brother will cast off profit and deal with one another with benevolence and righteousness in mind. No state like that has ever failed to attain true kingship. Why must you speak of profit?"

When Mencius was living in Zou, Ji Ren, who was acting as regent of Ren, sent him gifts of silk to make his acquaintance. Mencius accepted them and did not go to thank him. When he was living in Pinglu, Chuzi, who was chief minister of Qi, sent him gifts of silk to make his acquaintance. Mencius accepted them and did not go to thank him. Later, when he went from Zou to Ren, he visited Jizi; but when he went from Pinglu to the capital of Qi, he did not visit Chuzi. Wulu Zi was delighted and said, "Here is my opening!" He asked, "Master, when you went to Ren you visited Jizi, but when you went to Qi you did not visit Chuzi. Was it because Chuzi was only a minister?" Mencius said, "No. The Book of Documents says, 'In offering gifts, ceremony matters most. If the ceremony falls short of the things offered, it is called no offering, for the heart was not put into the offering.' It was because his offering was not properly made." Wulu Zi was pleased. When someone asked him about it, Wulu Zi said, "Jizi could not go to Zou [being regent], but Chuzi could have gone to Pinglu."

Chunyu Kun said, "To put reputation and achievement first is to work for others; to put them last is to work for oneself. You, Master, were among the three high ministers of Qi, yet you left before your reputation and achievement had reached either the ruler above or the people below. Is that really how a benevolent man behaves?" Mencius said, "Staying in a low position and refusing to serve an unworthy ruler with his worth: that was Bo Yi. Going five times to Tang and five times to Jie: that was Yi Yin. Not disdaining a corrupt ruler and not declining a small office: that was Liuxia Hui. These three followed different paths, but their aim was one. What was that one thing? Benevolence. The gentleman need only be benevolent; why must he act the same as others?" "In the time of Duke Mu of Lu, Gongyi Zi was in charge of the government and Ziliu and Zisi were ministers, yet Lu lost more territory than ever. So this is how little benefit worthy men bring to a state!" Mencius said, "Yu did not employ Baili Xi and perished; Duke Mu of Qin employed him and became overlord. If a state does not employ worthy men it perishes; how could it get off with merely losing territory?" Chunyu Kun said, "Formerly, when Wang Bao lived on the Qi River, the people west of the Yellow River became good at chanting; when Mian Ju lived in Gaotang, the people of western Qi became good at singing; the wives of Hua Zhou and Qi Liang wept so well for their husbands that they changed the customs of the state. What is within must show itself without. I have never seen anyone do the work without achieving the result. Therefore there are no worthy men; if there were, I would surely know of them." Mencius said, "When Confucius was minister of justice in Lu, his advice was not followed. He attended a sacrifice, and when his portion of the sacrificial meat was not sent to him, he left without even taking off his ceremonial cap. Those who did not understand him thought it was because of the meat; those who understood a little thought it was because of the breach of ritual. In fact, Confucius wanted to leave on account of a slight fault [of the ruler's], and did not want to leave without good reason. What the gentleman does is beyond the understanding of the common run of people."

Mencius said, "The five overlords were offenders against the three kings; the feudal lords of today are offenders against the five overlords; and the great officers of today are offenders against the feudal lords of today. When the Son of Heaven visited the feudal lords it was called a tour of inspection; when the feudal lords attended the court of the Son of Heaven it was called reporting on their duties. In spring he inspected the ploughing and supplemented what was lacking; in autumn he inspected the harvest and helped those who did not have enough. If on entering a state he found the land opened up, the fields well tended, the old cared for, the worthy honored, and men of talent in office, then there was a reward, and the reward was land. If on entering a state he found the land neglected and overgrown, the old abandoned, the worthy overlooked, and grasping men in office, then there was a reprimand. If a lord failed once to attend court, he was lowered in rank; if he failed twice, his territory was reduced; if he failed three times, the six armies were sent against him. Thus the Son of Heaven punishes but does not attack, while the feudal lords attack but do not punish. The five overlords dragged feudal lords along to attack other feudal lords; hence I say the five overlords were offenders against the three kings. Of the five overlords, Duke Huan was the greatest. At the meeting of the feudal lords at Kuiqiu, he bound the sacrificial animal and placed the written covenant on it, but did not smear the lips with blood. The first article said, 'Punish the unfilial; do not change the appointed heir; do not make a concubine your wife.' The second said, 'Honor the worthy and nurture talent, so as to make the virtuous known.' The third said, 'Respect the old and be kind to the young; do not neglect guests and travelers.' The fourth said, 'Let no office be hereditary; let no one hold two offices at once; in choosing officers, be sure to get the right men; do not put a great officer to death on your own authority.' The fifth said, 'Do not build dikes that divert the water [onto others]; do not stop the sale of grain; do not make any grant of land without reporting it.' And it said, 'All of us who have joined in this covenant, now that we have sworn it, will return to good relations.' The feudal lords of today all break these five prohibitions; hence I say the feudal lords of today are offenders against the five overlords. To encourage a ruler in his wickedness is a small offense; to anticipate a ruler's wickedness and lead him into it is a great offense. The great officers of today all anticipate their rulers' wickedness; hence I say the great officers of today are offenders against the feudal lords of today."

Lu wanted to make Shenzi commander of its army. Mencius said, "To use the people in war without having first instructed them is called bringing calamity on the people. One who brought calamity on the people would not have been tolerated in the age of Yao and Shun. Even if you defeated Qi in a single battle and so took possession of Nanyang, it would still not be right." Shenzi flushed with displeasure and said, "This is something I, Huali, do not understand." Mencius said, "I will tell you plainly. The territory of the Son of Heaven is a thousand li square; with less than a thousand li he would not have enough to receive the feudal lords. The territory of a feudal lord is a hundred li square; with less than a hundred li he would not have enough to maintain the statutes of his ancestral temple. When the Duke of Zhou was enfeoffed in Lu, it was with a hundred li square; it was not that there was not enough land, but it was limited to a hundred li. When the Grand Duke was enfeoffed in Qi, it was also with a hundred li square; it was not that there was not enough land, but it was limited to a hundred li. Now Lu is five times a hundred li square. If a true king arose, do you think Lu would be among those whose territory is reduced, or among those whose territory is increased? Even simply taking land from one state to give to another is something a benevolent man would not do; how much less would he seek it by killing people! The gentleman, in serving his ruler, strives only to lead his ruler onto the right Way and to set his mind on benevolence."

Mencius said, "Those who serve rulers today say, 'I can open up new lands for my ruler and fill his treasuries.' The so-called good ministers of today are what the ancients called robbers of the people. If the ruler does not turn toward the Way or set his mind on benevolence, and one tries to make him rich, that is enriching a Jie. They say, 'I can make alliances for my ruler with other states, and win every war.' The so-called good ministers of today are what the ancients called robbers of the people. If the ruler does not turn toward the Way or set his mind on benevolence, and one tries to make him strong in war, that is assisting a Jie. Following the way of today, without changing the customs of today, even if one were given the whole world one could not hold it for a single morning."

Bai Gui said, "I would like to take one part in twenty as tax. What do you think?" Mencius said, "Your way is the way of the Mo barbarians. In a state of ten thousand households, would it do to have only one potter?" "No, there would not be enough vessels to use." "In the land of the Mo, the five grains do not grow, only millet. They have no city walls, palaces, ancestral temples, or sacrificial rites; no gifts of silk or banquets for the feudal lords; and no hundred officials and departments. So one part in twenty is enough for them. But we live in the Central States. How could we do away with human relations and have no gentlemen? If a state cannot be run with too few potters, how much less without gentlemen! Those who want to make the tax lighter than the way of Yao and Shun are greater or lesser Mo barbarians; those who want to make it heavier than the way of Yao and Shun are greater or lesser Jies."

Bai Gui said, "My management of the waters is better than Yu's." Mencius said, "You are mistaken. Yu's management of the waters followed the way of water. So Yu used the four seas as his drain, while you use neighboring states as your drain. When water flows against its course it is called a deluge, and a deluge is a flood, which a benevolent man hates. You are mistaken."
Mencius said, "If a gentleman is not faithful to his word, how can he hold firm to anything?"

Lu wanted to put Yuezheng Zi in charge of the government. Mencius said, "When I heard of it, I was so happy I could not sleep." Gongsun Chou said, "Is Yuezheng Zi a man of strength?" "No." "Is he wise and far-seeing?" "No." "Is he widely learned?" "No." "Then why were you so happy you could not sleep?" "He is a man who loves goodness." "Is loving goodness enough?" "Loving goodness is more than enough to govern the whole world, let alone the state of Lu. If a man truly loves goodness, people from everywhere within the four seas will think nothing of coming a thousand li to tell him what is good. If he does not love goodness, people will say of him, 'Self-satisfied: he thinks he knows it all already.' That self-satisfied tone and look keeps people a thousand li away. When scholars stop a thousand li away, slanderers, flatterers, and sycophants arrive. If one lives among slanderers, flatterers, and sycophants, can the state be well governed, however one may wish it?"

Chenzi said, "Under what conditions did the gentlemen of old take office?" Mencius said, "There were three conditions for taking office and three for leaving. If he was received with the utmost respect and proper courtesy, and told that his words would be put into practice, he took office. If the courtesy did not lessen but his words were not put into practice, he left. Next, even if his words were not put into practice, if he was received with the utmost respect and proper courtesy, he took office; when the courtesy lessened, he left. Lowest of all, if he had nothing to eat morning or evening and was so faint with hunger that he could not go out of his door, and the ruler, hearing of it, said, 'I cannot in the larger matter put his Way into practice, nor can I follow his words, but I would be ashamed to let him starve in my land,' and relieved his need, then he might accept it, but only to avoid death."

Mencius said, "Shun rose up from the fields; Fu Yue was raised to office from among the builders of walls; Jiao Ge from among the sellers of fish and salt; Guan Yiwu from the hands of the jailer; Sunshu Ao from the seashore; and Baili Xi from the marketplace. So when Heaven is about to lay a great task on a person, it first frustrates his heart and will, wearies his sinews and bones, starves his body, leaves him destitute, and confounds whatever he undertakes, so as to stir his heart, toughen his nature, and make up for what he is unable to do. People commonly make mistakes, and only then can they correct them. They are distressed in heart and blocked in their plans, and only then do they rise up. It shows in their faces and comes out in their voices, and only then are they understood. A state that has no law-abiding families and upright counselors within, and no rival states or foreign threats without, will commonly perish. From this we know that we live through sorrow and adversity and die through ease and pleasure."
Mencius said, "There are many methods of teaching. When I refuse to teach someone, that too is a way of teaching him."
